title: [Note: ADM 137/3621A-3621E are produced as a single document: order as ADM 137/3621 ]. Folios...
description: [Note: ADM 137/3621A-3621E are produced as a single document: order as ADM 137/3621 ]. Folios 1-14 and 16: missing or blank. Folio 15-23: Signals. Cover (folio 15). Folio 17: Number 395. 26 May 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C SECRET. Lord Kitchener is proceeding to Archangel with mission consisting of Brig. General Ellershaw, Sir F. Donaldson, Colonel Fitzgerald, Mr. Obeirne Foreign Office, a Junior Officer and six servants. The Mission leaving London by train on 5 June and to leave Scapa Flow on evening of 6 June. A cruiser to take the Mission from Scapa to Archangel. Folio 17: Number 941. 27 May 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. Proposing HMS Hampshire and asking if coal will be available at Archangel, if not speed will be about 13 knots. Folio 17: Number 403. 27 May 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. HMS Hampshire is suitable and a collier will be sent to Yukanskie. Folio 17: Number 947. 27 May 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. Enquiring if HMS Hampshire is to wait at Yukanskie. Folio 17: Number 411. 28 May 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Collier sailed to Yukanskie and also coal available there. Missions return date unknown so probability HMS Hampshire will not have to wait. Folio 17: Number 440. 2 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Lord Kitchener wants to board HMS Hampshire at Thurso. Folio 17: Number 35. 4 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty that above is undesirable owing to submarine danger and should come over [to Scapa] by destroyer. Folio 18: Number 495. 4 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Lord Kitchener arriving Thurso morning of 5 June 1916 and destroyer approved. Folio 18: Number 51. 5 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. Lord Kitchener will return to Archangel about 21 June. Propose HMS Hampshire to wait there and collier sent to replenish coal used. Folio 18: Number 514. 5 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C and C-in-C to HMS Hampshire. Approve waiting and confirming collier sent. Folio 18: Number 57. 5 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. By what code or cypher can HMS Hampshire communicate by W/T with HMS Iphigenia. Folio 18: Number 61. 6 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. Deeply regret to report that HMS Hampshire with Lord Kitchener and staff on board was sunk by mine or torpedo off Brough of Birsay, west side of Orkney about 8.0 p.m. last night. Heavy seas were running. Searching at sea and ashore. Fear that there will be no survivors. Folio 19: Number 522. 6 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Lord Kitchener had number of most secret papers. Search floating wreckage and coast. Folio 19: Number 65. 6 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. This was already arranged. Folio 19: Number 68 6 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. All hopes of mission being saved must be abandoned. Thirteen survivors ashore, one since died. Among bodies 2nd Lieutenant Macpherson on staff as Russian interpreter. Folio 19: Number 69. 6 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. All communications between Orkneys and Main Land suspended as information regarding Lord Kitchener will not yet be published. Of great importance not to give position of sinking. Folio 19: Number 528. 6 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Further stoppage of communication is not essential. Folio 19: Number 76. 6 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. Body of Colonel Fitzgerald and over 100 bodies of crew recovered. Are bodies of Fitzgerald and Macpherson to be buried here? Folio 20: Number 529. 6 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Admiralty announces that HMS Hampshire, Captain Herbert J. Savill, with Lord Kitchener and his staff was sunk last night, west of Orkney by mine or torpedo. Four boats were seen to leave the ship but as a heavy sea was running, only some bodies have been found, and there is little hope of there being any survivors. Folio 21: Number 541. 7 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. The War Office has ascertained that Lieutenant Macpherson is to be buried locally and Colonel Fitzgerald's body is to be brought to London. Folio 21: Number 100. 8 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. Moored mines found today in locality where HMS Hampshire sank. Folio 21: Number 563. 8 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. Cabinet asking for details so request by 1st Lord for report after survivors interviewed. Folio 21: Number 109. 8 June 1916, C-in-C to Admiralty. For First Lord, report is due at Admiralty tomorrow by messenger. Folio 22: 22 June 1916, C-in-C to Rear Admiral 2nd Cruiser Squadron. Forward list of bodies from HMS Hampshire stating where buried. Folio 22: Number 725. 22 June 1916, Admiralty to C-in-C. For probate, names required of Lord Kitchener's staff and their attendants embarking on HMS Hampshire. Otherwise, ascertain composition of party on passing Inverness or at Thurso. S.N.O. Inverness to Admiralty. Nothing known of party passing Inverness. Folio 22: Rear Admiral 2nd Cruiser Squadron to C-in-C. Have no information as to bodies recovered but have requested Rear Admiral Scapa to forward list to you and Admiralty. Folio 22: Rear Admiral Scapa to C-in-C. Have furnished Admiralty with all particulars, am forwarding list to you for your information. Folio 22: C-in-C to Rear Admiral Scapa. Ascertain from Alouette retinue of Lord Kitchener: names, description or status, and number. Folio 23: 24 June 1916, Rear Admiral Cyclops to C-in-C. Alouette reports names not take. As far as can be recollected, 6 crossed over with 4 in khaki and 2 in civilian clothes. The 4 in khaki included Detective Sergeant McLaughlin, Driver Brown, Lord Kitchener's personal servant, and Sir F. Donaldson's servant. Thurso reported 7 not 6 embarked. Folio 23: Number 269. C-in-C to Admiralty. Gentlemen named in letter of 7 June 1916 and in addition Mr Leslie Robertson lunched with C-in-C on 5 June 1916 and sailed in HMS Hampshire. Folio 24: Telegram, 6 June 1916 from Senior Officer 2nd Cruiser Squadron to C-in-C. Temporary Surgeon Lieutenant Arthur Riddle, HMS Hampshire, proceeded on leave 4 June 1916. Folio 25: Admiralty to C-in-C, 7 Oct. 1916, forwarded to Vice Admiral Commanding Orkney and Shetland. For probate purposes, who identified body of Colonel Fitzgerald? Reply 9 October. Identified through uniform and by personal belongings by Surgeon Bainbridge and E. J. Lincoln of hospital ship Soudan. Folios 26-46: Naval Signals concerning search for bodies and wreckage also number of survivors. Folios 47-49: No 10 H, SECRET, 5 June 1916 from Vice Admiral Frederic Edward Errington Brock, commander Orkney and Shetland to C-in-C. Cover (folio 47). 1. At 8.p.m. received a report from Captain Walker, Officer Commanding Western Patrol that a battle cruiser appeared to be in difficulties between Brough of Birsay and Marwick Head. Thought it probable to be Hampshire getting into heavy seas but ordered a yacht and trawler to be in readiness. 2. At 8.35p.m. Captain Walker reported 'ship down'. He had already directed all available vessels to the scene. Ordered to send to Birsay any motor vehicle available at Stromness. 3. At 8.50p.m. I received a message from Birsay that a four funnelled cruiser had sunk twenty minutes earlier. 4. At 9.p.m. directed Colonel G Harris R.M.A. to proceed to Birsay and he left at once with Commander Bertram Nicholson, Commanding the Northern Patrols. 5. At 9.08 p.m. report that 4 boat loads of people were off Marwick Head. I directed that all inhabitants along the coast to assist. 6. Between 9.35 and 9.40 p.m. all destroyers sent by your orders passed through Hoy Sound. Listing continued in ADM 137/3621B.

title: Folios 100-101: James Hanway Plumridge, HM Sloop Sappho, Portsmouth. Reply to Admiralty letter of 18...
description: Folios 100-101: James Hanway Plumridge, HM Sloop Sappho, Portsmouth. Reply to Admiralty letter of 18 April 1820, which had enclosed a copy of a letter from the Right Honourable Lord Charles Somerset to Mr Goulborn. Refers them to the letters he sent earlier, together with his orders from the Commander in Chief, which he is sure will satisfy their Lordships that he in no way exceeded his instructions. Goes on to describe the nature of the arrangement by which he gave passage to his lordship and family, the offer of some expenses for the table from his lordship, and the fact that he brought stock on board, and encouraged Captain Plumridge to invite whomever he wished to dinner. Plumridge says this was all in the nature of a private and friendly arrangement and does not alter the circumstances of his having to provide for his guests. Admiralty note on rear not easy to decipher as crossed over writing, but seems to indicate their view that Lord Somerset bore the brunt of his own expenses.

title: Folios 194-195: James Nicoll Morris (late of HMS Formidable), London. He is complying with Admiralty...
description: Folios 194-195: James Nicoll Morris (late of HMS Formidable), London. He is complying with Admiralty directions of 17 June to comment on Mr Evan Evans's letter and to assure them the Service will not suffer in any way by the discharge of this midshipman. He says the young man was originally before the mast in the Formidable, but his conduct in bearing a serious wound that was not only painful but gave him daily apprehension that his hand would need to be amputated first brought him to Morris's notice. He found Evans had some knowledge of mathematics so when he returned from hospital he was rated midshipman to teach the young officers navigation. When the ship was paid off he expressed a desire to pass for Master, and with the Admiral's leave Morris sent him to London. However circumstances [difficult to decipher] meant he could not take his exam but went as midshipman in the Queen Charlotte. Morris thinks he would make a good master if he could take the exam but points out he will never recover the full use of his hand or be entirely free from pain. Adds he knows nothing of the young man's personal background but his conduct has always been good and sober.

title: Folios 303-304: Donald McLeod, Regulating Captain, Liverpool. Replying to Admiralty query dated 15 July, he...
description: Folios 303-304: Donald McLeod, Regulating Captain, Liverpool. Replying to Admiralty query dated 15 July, he says that Aaron Richards was a black man impressed by Lt Evans on 11 July as an ordinary (shipwright) aged 20, born in Halifax. He had arrived here in an American vessel, the Traveller and her master claimed to be instructing him in the art of navigation, but as he is a British subject McLeod felt it his duty to impress him. A second letter of the same date had asked him to send an affidavit of what was said by Williams re Charles Cutter. McLeod says that the landlady where they both lodged says Williams went to sea about 3 weeks ago in the Dryad, Captain Parker, expected back in about 3 months. Asked what she knew about Cutter she said he always called himself Alex and she understood his surname to be Jones, and supposed he was Welsh. As for Arthur Nunnery, who was to be surveyed by a surgeon, he has been drafted from the Princess for Passage to Plymouth. Folios 305-306: enclosure with folios 303-304. Letter dated 13 July 1811 by William Rathbone, Liverpool, saying that Aaron Richards' story is one of peculiar hardship and that he was taken as an apprentice by the owner of the American brig Traveller, to instruct him and eventually return him to his parents. This letter is hard to decipher and lengthy but is requesting Richards's release.

title: Folios 142-148: Sir John Phillimore, Orton Atherstone, Warwickshire. Writes with regard to his knighthood, having...
description: Folios 142-148: Sir John Phillimore, Orton Atherstone, Warwickshire. Writes with regard to his knighthood, having received their letter of 28 May which he says indicated that judging by the report in the Dublin Gazette, their Lordships had doubts over the legality of his title. He notes that in their letter of 29 December last, they had noted the KCB attached to his name and assumed it to be an error of his clerk's. Expresses some grievance over the fact that his conduct has been in the past misrepresented to them, also that others who have had such titles conferred on them have not been so doubted. Expounds at length on the authenticity of his title, and his anxiety to do away with any doubts. He had been removed from the command of the yacht William and Mary, which he describes as 'unprecedented'. and notes that it was not by the desire of the Lord Lieutenant Marquis Wellesley, but believes something he did had displeased the Lord Lieutenant Earl Talbot. There follows an extensive account of his actions and the conduct of others while he was in command of the yacht in Dublin harbour. He and his officers had been insulted in various ways by the harbour master and by the mayor, the midshipmen accused of drunkenness etc, though witnesses said they were sober. A very unsatisfactory enquiry had been held as to his own conduct. He points out that the command of the William and Mary was his first after being in hospital for six months after being wounded. He has been in great pecuniary difficulty since. Thus the knighthood conferred on him by the Lord Lieutenant, which should be a mark of esteem, he says, has been converted into a mark of ridicule and disgrace. A lengthy response from the Admiralty follows, difficult to decipher [would repay study] but seems to say their Lordships had not been displeased with him.

title: Folios 276-277: William Taylor, HMS La Prompte, in Leith Roads. Advising of his arrival at...
description: Folios 276-277: William Taylor, HMS La Prompte, in Leith Roads. Advising of his arrival at this place the previous evening, having sailed from Flushing on 20 October, as he had written to tell them. He intends to complete the ship's water and stores, and repairs, including the caulking which was damaged in recent gales, then proceed to the south as per his orders. He has had news from a revenue cutter here, of HMS Resolution, currently cruising at the mouth of the Firth, and in case she doesn't appear before he leaves he will leave instructions for her to follow him, to meet at Kirkwall or Lerwick. Other information he has had from a merchant ship from the Baltic, of two French frigates, a brig and a cutter, in the South Seas, and from a Newcastle ship, that a vessel from Norway had arrived there and had struck to four French frigates and a two-decker, but owing to bad weather had managed to escape. Also intelligence from a sloop that arrived at Leith yesterday, from Bergen, that there were four French frigates with several prizes, intending to make for Dunkirk. Encloses monthly journal and state and condition of ship [not present]. Folio 278: enclosure with folios 276-277. Admiralty note on a scrap of paper, not very decipherable.

title: Folios 370-371: Thomas Cochrane (Earl), 13 Green Street. Has received Admiralty letter of 17 March...
description: Folios 370-371: Thomas Cochrane (Earl), 13 Green Street. Has received Admiralty letter of 17 March informing him that their Lordships now decline to enter into any 'detailed examination' regarding his supposed involvement in the Stock Exchange fraud. He has therefore taken the trouble to collect a good deal of information for their consideration - as the case stands he says they have 'virtually given judgement' and superseded him from his command, on 'no better foundation than declarations retailed from pot houses and such like places from persons not upon oath, which given in the absence of the accused are absurd and contradictory'. Refers to the evidence of the Committee of the Stock Exchange as 'a tissue of misrepresentation from one end to the other'. Folios 372-373: enclosure with folios 370-371. To Cochrane, in response to his letter of 22 March, initialled only and referring him to an earlier letter of 17 March, saying their Lordships have nothing to add, some hard to decipher remarks about the Stock Exchange and ending by saying that in Cochrane's absence an Acting [underlined] captain was to be appointed to HMS Tonnant, the choice of officer to be made by Cochrane. Folio 374:enclosure with folios 370-371. Sworn statement from Samuel Thomas of 102 Bank Buildings, Cornhill, successor to Binns & Co, that he never sold any foreign or other coin to Lord Cochrane, or had any other transaction with him. Folios 375-376: enclosure with folios 370-371. Sworn statement from Thomas Dewman that he was hired by Lord Cochrane to go to the country and relieve his steward, and on 21 February a gentleman came while his Lordship was out. He told this man it was unlikely Lord Cochrane would be back before dinner and the man said it was urgent, so Dewman agreed to take a note to Cochrane, whom he found at Mr King's Tin manufactory in Cock Lane. Dewman describes the man who sent him, an officer in a grey regimental greatcoat etc., the only military man who came to the house. No one stayed at that house except his Lordship, nor did any of the men described by the policeman, Sayer, or by the hackney coachman, Crane, ever come to his Lordship's house at 13 Green Street while Dewman was there. Folios 377-378: enclosure with folios 370-371. Sworn statement from Isaac Davies, who was in Cochrane's service on 21 February, when several gentlemen came to the house in Green Street, including a Captain Berenger, wearing a grey greatcoat. Also says no man lived in the house except his Lordship and servants, and that he never saw anyone like the man described by Crane at the house. Folios 379-380: enclosure with folios 370-371. Sworn statement of Mary Turpin, who was cookmaid Lord Cochrane, that she saw an officer in the parlour at Green Street on 21 February, wearing a grey greatcoat and sword. Adds that no one but his lordship lived in the house except his servants. Folios 381-382: enclosure with folios 370-371. Sworn statement of Robert Wale King, 1 Cock Lane, tin manufacturer, that on 21 February Lord Cochrane had come there to oversee the construction of his patent lanterns, and that while he was there he received a note, read it and left.

title: Folios 516-517: Edward Rotherham, HMS Lapwing in the Downs. Advising that William Doyle, a prisoner...
description: Folios 516-517: Edward Rotherham, HMS Lapwing in the Downs. Advising that William Doyle, a prisoner whom Lord Hugh Seymour had ordered him to give passage to, had as they came into the Channel jumped into the sea 'in a fit of frenzy' and drowned himself. Folios 518-519: enclosure with folios 516-517. From John Kelly[?] to John Dawson, from [?Penz]ance Island. In this difficult to decipher letter, John Kelly refers to one of John Dawson's letters to Thomas Powell in which he says he is about to leave Liverpool for the West Indies and Kelly is confident that Dawson has a good knowledge of the African trade and would be the best person to deal with what he calls a 'villainous action' lately taken place. He says a Captain Doyle, of a schooner formerly named the Demeral[?], at present belonging to Trinidad, had chased a Portuguese sloop, taken possession of her and her 16 or 17 people and had put them in irons, intending to take them to the West Indies - he is hoping whichever island they go to the people there will take notice of what the captives say and is sure that if the man goes unpunished and the captives are not returned it will have serious consequences for trade in those parts. The same man had chased a vessel of Mr Irving's [?] and took 40 slaves from her which he 'paid for his own way'. There is also a report he had shot one of his people. Asks Dawson to make this business 'as public as you can' and says he himself has written to the governor of Barbados and several others. Asks if a vessel may be sent out to collect what goods of Dawson's remain in Mr Powell's hands. Folio 520: enclosure with folios 516-517. Slip of paper with a list of ivory, by weight. Folios 521-521A: enclosure with folios 516-517. Cover wrapper for 'papers relating to the Portuguese sloop captured by the schooner Lancaster, William Doyle Master'. Folios 522-523: enclosure with folios 516-517. From Thomas Powell to Captain Doyle, Isles de Los, 21 May 1800, saying he is sorry Doyle is unwell and advising that he will send 'the remainder of the rice' if Doyle sends a boat. Asks in return for quantities of various goods, with indigenous names. Advises him if he goes upriver not to leave his vessel, because of the account that might be given by some of the Portuguese he has on board, who 'suppose that you assisted in taking them' and might seek to avenge themselves somehow. Also sends him some cheese he has found in store. Folios 524-525: enclosure with folios 516-517. Port of Spain, Trinidad, 4 July 1800. Examination of the master and crew, 'all free negroes belonging to a Portuguese sloop piratically captured by the schooner Lancaster' on the coast of Africa, April, the case taken before John Nugent, one of the Island judges. Domingo Suares, master of the Portuguese sloop the Nostra Senora de la Carmen, describes their voyage towards Sierra Leone a few months previously, having aboard 12 large 'elephants' teeth', yams and other items, when they were stopped and asked for trade by the Lancaster schooner. Four men went aboard the schooner with some of the goods, and he joined them to make the exchange but felt the captain was not dealing fairly with them so returned. Then the captain of the Lancaster gave orders for the sloop to be boarded, the crew were taken captive and put in irons. Some of the men were later sold as slaves. Various confirmatory signatures from other crew members at foot. Folios 526-547: enclosure with folios 516-517. Examination of the crewmen belonging to the Lancaster, William Doyle Master. Pierre Russe, a native of Brittany, was aboard the Lancaster with Mr Doyle as Master at Barbados, on 12 or 13 February 1800 and sailed for the coast of Africa. Near the Isle of Los he was ordered to go with the mate on board one of the boats to pursue a Portuguese sloop but they had to give up for lack of arms, and the schooner eventually returned with the men of the sloop on board, who were placed among the slaves. Similar detailed depositions from Matthias Bondee, from Sweden; George Walker, cabin boy; Duncan Dennis, of North Wales; Thomas Barnett, of Gloucester; William Cusey, North America; John Evans, S. Wales; William Cooke, of Ireland; George Creaner, of Philadelphia; George Jennerson, of Philadelphia; William Green of the Isle of Wight; Andrew Hanson, of Denmark; William Carney, of Ireland; Richard Sherman, of Liverpool; Thomas Hunter, of Scotland; John Watts, of Ireland, who recounts how they were asked if they would prefer going into the boat or in irons, and when Samuel White answered 'By the Holy Ghost he would sooner die' Captain Doyle shot him with a pistol. Some examinations with questions and answers follow each deposition, very detailed accounts with further information. Folio 548: enclosure with folios 516-517. List in Portuguese, possibly a bill for stores, with values. Folio 549: enclosure with folios 516-517. Statement by three men, including George Creaner and John Watts, 17 May 1800, that Captain William Doyle had saved them from captivity and refused to hand them over to 'King Cantor' [one of the black crewmembers] who had taken a sloop named the Nancy, though he was urged to do so, and that he had no hand in taking that sloop.

title: Folios 249-250: James Hillyar, HMS Phoebe, Rio de Janeiro. Reports his arrival the previous evening...
description: Folios 249-250: James Hillyar, HMS Phoebe, Rio de Janeiro. Reports his arrival the previous evening with the ship he was ordered to escort, after a tedious voyage because that ship was such a poor sailer. Because of this it will be difficult to carry out his further orders. Recounts that while crossing the Bay of Biscay he had to take the ship in tow and was concerned that they would be driven onto a lee shore because she towed so badly. He has now delivered the packets he was carrying to Rear Admiral Manley Dixon. He left Santa Cruz on 5 April, and shortly afterwards was joined by the [Breah ?] and the [D E Baynes ?] which had become separated from their convoy. They stayed with him until 20 May when they parted company in Latitude 7º 23' South, Longitude 31º 30' West. Folios 251-252: enclosed with folios 249-250. Enciphered report, apparently from Captain James Hillyar, HMS Phoebe, covering several dates in 1813, which has been deciphered at the Admiralty. 16 July, Longitude 42º 59', Latitude 31° 5' South. Reports he opened his orders on 12 July and is proceeding with the Consort, HMS Cherub and HMS Raccoon to carry them out. Finds he is lacking the charts he needs, having only a single Admiralty chart of the Pacific Ocean but none of the Falcon [Falkland ?] Islands, Cape Horn, or the coasts of South America beyond Brazil. One of the sloops has neither chart nor timekeeper and they have no directions for entering the Colombia River. He has set the island of Juan Fernandez as the first rendezvous, Cocoa Island as the second and the River [Bound ?] as the last. 29 July. He has now decided to go to the first rendezvous, equip the Raccoon with six months' provisions and send her on alone while he goes looking for the enemy frigate. 29 September, off Lima. At Juan Fernandez he heard the enemy was at Valparaiso on 23 August but later spoke a Spanish brigantine which reported a frigate on the coast at Latitude 3º 28' and that there were prisoners there in great distress, so he has decided to call there to relieve them. The Raccoon has now parted company off Cape Blanco. 4 October. Arrived at the River [Tumbrel ?] and wrote to the Governor of Guyayaquil asking for information about the Englishmen, and on 11 October a messenger from the Governor told him the enemy was on this coast five weeks ago, had captured 13 ships and was believed to be going home, calling first on the coast of Chile, but other residents say they believe he is going back to the Gallapagos Islands. He will visit the islands and then go on to Lima. Reports that the Third Lieutenant, Purser, and one seaman have drowned. 14 October. Hears that the enemy frigate and several armed ships were seen off Lima 18 days earlier. Folios 253-254: enclosed with folios 249-250. Enciphered report, apparently from Captain James Hillyar, HMS Phoebe, Guayaquil, 1813, which has been deciphered at the Admiralty. He went to the Gallapagos Islands and returned here on the 3rd [month not clear]. The Viceroy says the enemy frigate was being blockaded by English ships on the Brazil coast. He has demanded restitution for the British ships and property, but power rests with the maritime department, whose decisions are sent to the Spanish court. Once he has secured provisions he intends to call at Valparaiso. The Commander of Marines appears to have great influence. [undated] Writes from Lima, where provisions are scarce but [not ?] naval stores. HMS Cherub is with him. Folios 255-258: enclosed with folios 249-250. Copies and translations of correspondence between Captain James Hillyar, HMS Phoebe in Callao Bay, and The Marquis of Concordia, Viceroy of Peru, and Don Joseph Pasqual de Vivero, Commandant of Marines, Lima, between 9 and 17 December 1813, concerning British ships the Boriska , the Hunter, O Russell, Master, and the Hector, captured by privateers the Vulture, whose commander Don Domingo Amezaga is accused of mistreating his prisoners, and the Santa Terese. [There is also a passing reference to a second vessel also called the Hunter, Mr Crabtree, Master.] Folios 259-260: enclosed with folios 249-250. Letter from John McDonald, HMS Phoebe, at sea, to Captain James Hillyar, 26 August 1813. Feels that their slow passage from England and the information they received at Rio de Janeiro have affected the mission Captain Hillyar was given to go to the Colombia River. Postscript. When he was in London he was acquainted with the orders given to Captain Hillyar, but he feels the length of their slow passage from England means that the season is far advanced, and from information he received from a native of the Sandwich Islands who had been into the river two years earlier, he does not think there will be sufficient water over the bar to allow a frigate to enter during winter, suggests he sends one of the sloops in his place. Believes that was the original intention until the possibility of the Isaac Todd not meeting one of the sloops was raised. Thinks Captain Hillyar would be better advised to remain off the Spanish coast to deal with the enemy, particularly the American frigate the Essex. Suggests a council of war between himself, the Captain and Mr McTavish. Folio 261: enclosed with folios 249-250. Letter from Captain James Hillyar, Lima, to the Admiralty, [?] January 1814. Reports that because communications are precarious, he has sent copies of his reports and of the letter from Mr McDonald which, together with the issue of provisions, led him to deviate from his orders. Hopes to sail on 11 January with HMS Cherub and with four months provisions. He has received reports that the insurgent army under General Manuel Belgrano has been dispersed, but has no news from Chile. He understands that the enemy have fitted out two or three of their prizes as sloops of war. Postscript. He will escort HMS Indispensable off the coast. Folios 262-263: enclosed with folios 249-250. [Marked as Duplicate] Letter from Captain James Hillyar, Lima, to the Admiralty, 23 December 1813. As the Viceroy has offered to forward his letter with his own despatches, is sending copies of their correspondence about the confiscated British ships and property. The Viceroy says decisions about these are in the jurisdiction of the Admiralty court in Spain, and that he has never given any orders regarding the Boriska. Had already reported in his letter of 8 December that he sailed from the River Tumbez in the Gulph of Guayaquil on 14 October, visited the Galapagos Islands and then arrived at Lima to be informed by the Viceroy that the Essex was blockaded in St Catherines. He is likely to be held at Lima for another two weeks in order to get a supply of bread. Thinks a British warship constantly on the coast of Peru would check the operations of cruizers.

title: Secret packs of the Commander in Chief Grand Fleet, Volume XXXVII, pack 0020, sections X-XIV....
description: Secret packs of the Commander in Chief Grand Fleet, Volume XXXVII, pack 0020, sections X-XIV. Trade - The Blockade. Folios 1: Title page. Folio 2: Explanatory note During the period of the War, papers of a confidential nature in the office of the C-in-C Home Fleet were filed in Packs (numbered separately from the non-confidential records) in a Series 001 to 0042 inclusive. Copies of relevant telegrams were filed in these packs, but a complete set of all telegrams was also maintained. The secret packs were re-arranged by the Grand Fleet secretarial staff in February 1919, when papers considered unimportant were removed and destroyed, and the remainder re-indexed. They were received in this form by the Historical Section in April 1920, and bound as received, in a series of Volumes. The 1919 index will be found in the first volume (see ADM 137/1881) and extracts from these have been inserted in each succeeding volume. This volume is the 37th of the series. Folio 3: Index of contents. Trade - The Blockade. Folios 4-7: Blank Folios 8: Sub-title page. Section X - The establishment of additional ports for the examination of neutral vessels and papers relating to their operation (folios 9-139). Folios 9-49: (a) Lerwick. Folios 50-82: (b) Loch Ewe. Folios 83-94: (c) Stornoway. Folios 95-139: (d) Kirkwall Folio 140 Sub-title page. Section XI - Protection of merchant shipping (folios 141-211A). Folios 141-211: Protection of merchant shipping including their markings, colours, disguises, neutral flags. Report regarding the loss of allied and neutral shipping in tonnages during October  December 1916 (folios 178-183). Norwegian shipping agreement and its operation (folios 201-211A). Folio 212: Sub-title page. Section XII - Armed Guards and reports of ships sent in for examination (folios 212-284). Folios 213-284: Armed guards (procedures to be adopted) and reports of ships sent in for examination. Interception by German submarines of neutral ships with British armed guards on board (folios 249-284). Letter dated 20 August 1915 by Sub Lieutenant H. Harris, Royal Naval Reserve, prisoner of war at Paderborn concerning the capture of the American ship, Pass of Balmaha. (folios 254-255). Sinking of the Norwegian SS Stralsund (folios 264-269). Sinking of the Norwegian ship Fiorella (folios 270-273). Interception of the Norwegian SS Hiso (folios 274-277). Instructions for Armed Guards (folios 278-284). Folio 285: Sub-title page. Section XIII - Trade Statistics (folios 286-384). Folios 286-384: Trade statistics. Tonnage of British munitions shipped from United States of America to the United Kingdom, France (rails) and Salonika (railway material), folio 286). Summary of personnel, horses and mules, supplies and explosives, vehicles and ships, sick and wounded, nursing sisters and civilians, refugees and prisoners from 9 August 1914 to 2 October 1916 (folio 287). Imports from Sweden (folio 288). Statistical notes for Lord Robert Cecil's speech to the Imperial Conference concerning imports into Scandinavia and Holland, exports of oils and fats from Holland to Germany during 1915-1916, exports of certain articles from Holland to Germany in 1915-1916 and a note on the declaration of cotton as contraband (folios 290-298). War Trade Statistical Department - memorandum on exports from Germany to Denmark, 1917, (folios 299-303). Draft agreement with the Swedish government (folios 306-319). The peace settlement in Europe (folios 319-322). Statement with regard to the Bloackade, Imperial Conference 1917 (folios 322-339). Memorandum dated 1 January 1917 in regard to the present position of the blockade (folios 340-347). Statement of the measures adopted to intercept the sea bourne commerce of Germany, Parliamentary paper, January 1916 (folios 347-351). Memorandum on the economic situation in the enemy countries, Imperial Conference 1917 (folios 351-358). Letter dated 26 January 1917 by Robert Cecil to Sir David Beatty - stating that he is anxious to work in the closest touch with the naval authorities (folios 359-360). Ministry of Munitions estimates of iron etc to be obtained from Sweden in 1917 (folios 361-363). A report on the impact of the blockade on Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Holland (folios 364-380). Statistics of imports into Scandinavia and Holland January to September 1916 (folios 381-383). Folio 385: Sub-title page. Section XIV. Enemy raiders (folios 386-587). Track chart showing the operations of the Emden between 10 September and 1 October 1914 (folio 390). Decyphers of telegrams and intelligence relating to the Appam dated 3 and 6 February 1916, (folios 393-397). Reports on the activities in February 1916 of the Pungo later known as the German Auxiliary cruiser Mowe (folios 398-406). Photographs of the German Auxiliary cruiser Mowe (folios 403-404, 406). The proposed use of decoy ships (folios 409-413). Suggestion that Special Service Colliers be armed with torpedoes (March 1916), (folio 416). Ships being fitted for conversion specifically the Prinz Friedrich Wilhelm and the Marie Horn (folios 417-418). Various proposals for the blockading of the North Sea (folios 421-438). Plans of suggested patrols to prevent enemy raiders breaking out of the North Sea (folios 449-450). Detailed appreciation report dated 30 October 1917 by the Plans Division of the situation as regards to German raiders (folios 492-506). Enemy raider Gamma (folios 507-578). Folios 513-554: missing. Capture of SS Yarrowdale including track chart (folios 555-557, 569-570, 573-576). Report of interview with American seamen C. D. Green and C. Quinn serving in the Yarrowdale (folios 558-568). Folios 588-591: Blank.

title: Folios 11-12: John Clements, Leith. Reports he has received intelligence from a Dutchman on board...
description: Folios 11-12: John Clements, Leith. Reports he has received intelligence from a Dutchman on board HMS Leith, formerly an Officer in the Prince of Orange's Marine Service, that he left a large ship at Greenock under Hamburg Colours called the Cesar and Peter bound from Hamburg to Mauritius. Whilst at Greenock the ship's papers were examined and the ship was found to be the property of Messrs. Parish and Co. of Hamburg. However, upon further examination it would appear the vessel is French and that the Bills of Lading did not correspond with the equipment on board. He therefore decided to proceed to Greenock to investigate but found that the vessel had sailed. He found Mr. Parish of Hamburg there. He was informed by the Dutchman that the fictitious Bills of Lading are made out in the name of Messrs. Parish and Co., but the proper Bills of Lading are written in code and kept in the possession of the Captain with the code being kept in Mauritius.

title: Venetian Manuscripts
description: These records formed part of a collection of Venetian state papers made by Rawdon Lubbock Brown, an English scholar resident in Venice for fifty years from 1833. Since 1862 he had been employed as an editor by the Public Record Office. There is an appreciable amount of copied or extracted material, some copied at the time of its production, some later (but before Brown's time), and the rest during his lifetime, often at the instigation of Italian friends who shared his interest in Venetian history. There is a significant amount of original material, in manuscript and print, which Brown started buying in the 1830s. The most important part of this, the Tiepolo-Contarini collection, in 80 lots,was purchased by him in 1837 for his compatriot Edward Cheney, who gave it to Brown in 1840. The importance of the collection lies in the light it throws on Venetian and European history, particularly in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, from ambassadorial despatches, reports, diaries, itineraries and from manuscript gazettes, avvisi, or newsletters reporting on Venice and all the capitals where the Republic was represented diplomatically. The superiority of the schematic reports (relazioni) made by Venetian ambassadors on their return from diplomatic service in any one country abroad or Italian state, and read by them in the Senate, was universally acknowledged at an early date, which accounts for the existence of copies of so many of them. The manuscript gazettes (riporti) were sold in Venice for a 'gazeta' (a coin) long before 1600; the earliest in this collection dates from 1634. This series contains diplomatic records which relate to the administrative history of Venice and its dependencies. These include ambassadors' reports and despatches; manuscript newsletters from European capitals; material on the career of Venetian ambassador Francesco Contarini (d 1624); documents in cypher; letters and instruments to and from the Senate (Pregadi); papers of the doges (some of which are brilliantly illuminated) and of the Grand Council and Council of Ten; records of the Inquisitors of State; and documents concerning Brown's own interest in Cervantes, Shakespeare, heretics and gypsies. There are also reports from local governors and captains, naval material, items relating to Englishmen in Venice and records of the State Inquisitors and Officio della Sanita. The policing of the city and the detail of community regulation of lighting and burial in Venice in the eighteenth century are documented, and there are lists of officials, such as ambassadors and procurators (proctors) of St Marks. The vast majority of these records are in Italian: a limited number of documents, usually formal, legal or papal or reproduced antiques are in Latin, a few in French or English, and very few in other European languages.

description: Correspondence, etc. Austrian Mission Official Archives (including litnographed copies of the twelve protocols of the Vienna Conference, 15 March-21 April 1855 The papers in boxes 18 (1 and 2) are in fifteen folded and tied packs and consist for the most part of despatches, drafts for despatches, telegram decyphers and copy memoranda (official archives) (See also F.O. General Correspondence before 1906, Austria; F.O. 7/461-465). Further papers, mainly private correspondence, respecting the mission are in PRO 30/22/12B-12D. The papers summarised give a valuable and detailed narrative, from the British side, of the planning and proceedings (and the failure) of the twelve meetings of the conference held in Vienna from 15 March to 21 April 1855.

Assuring his lordship that he is doing everything in his power to relieve him by a direct move and that he has reason to hope from the assurance given him this day by Admiral Graves that they may pass the Bar by 12 October. title: Government Code and Cypher School: Air Section: Reports on Italian and Other Foreign Air Forces (AS/AS- Series)
description: Intelligence reports on foreign (European) air forces produced by the Air Section. To aid the understanding of these reports, a number of working aids and orders of Battle are also included, also some correspondence files relating to the reports. The reports are copies of teleprinted reports to Service Ministries on the activities primarily of the Italian Air Force, both before and during the Second World War. Information on pre-war activities include operations in Spain during the Spanish Civil War, also activity in North Africa, the Aegean and Ethiopia. Information on war time activities includes operations in Africa, the Aegean, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily and mainland Italy, also operations in Russia. Information on other air force activities in reports comprises: the Spanish Air Forces (Nationalist and Insurgent) during the Spanish Civil War and the Spanish Air Forces subsequently between 1941 and 1945; some activity by the German Air Force in the Spanish Civil War and in and around Europe, prior to and in the early stages of the Second World War - operations by the German Air Forces in North Africa and the Mediterranean are to some extent covered by the Italian Air Force reporting; Russian operations in Finland in 1940; French activity in the Mediterranean, 1939-1943; Portuguese Air Force between August 1943 and October 1944 The reports describe combat operations, transport flights, accidents, deployments and other order of battle changes, readiness states of aircraft and air crews, fuel situations at individual airfields and attaché reports (those from the Italian Air Attaché in Tokyo described Japanese operations in the Far East). The reports are all based on decrypts of medium/low grade cipher messages: some are verbatim copies of translations while others are paraphrases of the original text.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Air Section: Reports on Italian and Other Foreign Air Forces (AS/AS- Series).

title: Folio 112: Downing to Bennet. Plague spreads in the United Provinces including `the best houses',...
description: Folio 112: Downing to Bennet. Plague spreads in the United Provinces including `the best houses', 905 deaths in Amsterdam alone. Dutch have lost hopes of gaining the alliance of Sweden and Denmark and are consequently unlikely to yield concessions to them. States accept Louis XIV's offer to mediate. Holland supplies ships to assist the Dutch West Indies Company. Dutch protest over Cape Verde presented to Downing. De Witt stifled debate over Cayana (Cayenne) since the Dutch do not wish to offend France. Dutch fear English may take over the West African gold and slave trade completely. Thinks Scotland's decision to prohibit all trade with the United Provinces for fear of contracting the plague is a wise one. Downing evades De Witt's request for a reply over Cape Verde and an official paper to protect the Dutch against the English fleet sailing to West Africa, suggesting that only an overall settlement will stop further hostilities there. Downing thinks an agreement would be advantageous to the Royal Africa Company but hopes that during the negotiations `Holmes will doe the work there', and does not believe the Dutch will hold to any agreement. `Never will be such a opportunity as this to make clear work in Africa.' Recalls earlier Dutch claim to the whole coast and trade of West Africa by Valkenburg. Date and place: 1660 Aug 4/14 Hague.
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: Folio 56: De Bacquoy to [Williamson]. Certain Provinces drag their feet in making contributions to...
description: Folio 56: De Bacquoy to [Williamson]. Certain Provinces drag their feet in making contributions to the defence effort which is led by Holland and West Friesland. States order those deputies concerned with the Dutch West Indies Company to make it comply with Danishrequest that it refrains from aggressive acts against the Danish Company's possessions in West Africa. The Dutch West Indies Company asks for return of property and compensation for English depredations in Cape Verde and Guinea. Dutch plan to manufacture more cannon. English threat to Dutch East Indies fleet. Danish and Swedish naval preparations probably directed against each other. Dutch Company's expedition to recapture Cape Verde. Russian delegation. Date and place: 1660 July 5 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: Folio 22: De Bacquoy to Bennet. Dutch do not wish to encourage privateers to such...
description: Folio 22: De Bacquoy to Bennet. Dutch do not wish to encourage privateers to such an extent that they find their pool of sailors too reduced. Zeeland's support for the Prince of Orange. Valkenburg's claim that all West Africa belongs to the Dutch and his incitement of a local king to capture Cormantin. Dutch military preparations. Dutch hasten to satisfy Swedish demands. De Ruyter may attack the English when he returns. Imprisonment of Dutch sailors in England may deter Dutchmen from volunteering as sailors, as also may the widespread support for the Prince of Orange. French merchants complain of English depredations on ships trading with the United Provinces. Dutch fear of English landings on their coast. Date and place: 1665 Jan 17 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: North Africa: GAF report for Nov 16, intentions for Nov 17; Kesselring's directive to GAF...
description: North Africa: GAF report for Nov 16, intentions for Nov 17; Kesselring's directive to GAF to support Panzer Army (see 1405); signal from Rommel underlining seriousness of fuel situation, identifies best harbour for small ships as Ras El Ali, Nov 16; explosion seen in Ras Aali roadstead; proposal that troops help immediate unloading of Hans Arp on arrival Benghazi. Summary of special intelligence reports on North Africa, Nov 16. No fuel for operational aircraft in Berca or Magrun, Nov 16. title: Folio 125: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. Boreel communicated to Louis XIV Dutch proposals regarding joint...
description: Folio 125: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. Boreel communicated to Louis XIV Dutch proposals regarding joint action against the Barbary pirates, and anxieties regarding restitution of Orange, and the persecution of Protestants in Piedmont. Louis XIV agrees to joint action against the Barbary pirates which might include English participation, and to providing port and provisioning facilities at Toulon for the Dutch. States General have written to the Admiralties strongly urging that sufficient forces be made available to `clean up' the Mediterranean. Many English and Dutch ships have been seized and taken into Algiers. Tromp has captured another Turkish (Barbary) pirate ship.` France reiterates requests for satisfaction of the claims of the Grand Master of Malta, and seconds the Bishop of Münster's representations for the restitution of Borkelo by the Count of Stirum. Dutch surprise that Downing has raised Danish complaints about the Dutch West Indies Company's activities in West Africa. Danish ambassador seems satisfied with Dutch reply to his complaints. States General wish their West India Company to allow Danes to trade freely to their possessions in West Africa, also they should be, where applicable, restored to Denmark, and claims for compensation satisfied. King of Denmark's liability to assist the Emperor in his capacity as Duke of Holstein. Report that Charles II is growing jealous of Louis XIV's power. Date and place: 1665 Feb 17 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: Folio 84: De Bacquoy to Bennet. De Lionne's complaint that all his communication to the...
description: Folio 84: De Bacquoy to Bennet. De Lionne's complaint that all his communication to the Dutch subsequently became available to public. Dutch are to see whether they can keep diplomatic correspondence secret. Dutch hopes that if the English attack in the Caribbean they will anger the French by damaging interests of Frenchmen in that area. Admiral Banckert instructed not to expose his fleet to undue risk. Disquiet amongst English aristocracy and merchants over the war. Impracticability of building forts in `Hitland' [?Shetlands] to prevent Dutch going round the north of Scotland. Dutch East Indies Company obtain prolongation of their octroi until 1700 in return for providing 20 warships. Dutch doubts whether France will honour her treaty obligations. French troop concentrations near Amiens supposedly [? in case of incursion of German troops into the Spanish Netherlands]. Dutch military preparations. Sweden agrees to abandon her claims in West Africa to the Dutch in return for 140,000 Rix dollars. France has 16,000 men in Champagne, threatening the Spanish Netherlands. This has compelled the Dutch to strengthen their forces in the South to guard against a sudden attack [from the French]. Van Beuningen is to try and extract a firm commitment from France. Report that De Ruyter has set off to invade Barbados, while a force of Zeelanders hope to seize les Virgines. Date and place: 1665 Feb 4/14 [Leeuwarden].
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: Folio 9: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. Dutchmen who wish to see the fall of De...
description: Folio 9: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. Dutchmen who wish to see the fall of De Witt and restoration of the Prince of Orange are delighted at indications that France will not honour its treaty obligation to the United Provinces, excusing itself by claiming that the Dutch expedition to West Africa provoked English aggression in the Channel. De Witt seems to be trying to encourage and arm Anabaptists and other frenetiques to rise up against Charles II. Hopes De Witt will be blamed for causing the war and for opposing the restitution of the Prince of Orange to the position he formerly held. Dutch Council of State recommends that a greater number of warships be made ready than recommended previously. It is proposed to send three deputies from the States General and a deputy from each of the Admiralties aboard the Dutch fleet to ensure better discipline and determination. France may support Dutch. Dutch will cashier English and Scottish soldiers in their pay. Zeeland wants letters of marque to be issued; fears that if this is delayed, potential privateers assembled at Ostend may join the English side. English have apparently already issued letters of marque. De Ruyter' success on West African coast; he is expected to head for home soon. France prevaricates in reply to Dutch request for assistance. Date and place: 1665 Jan 3 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: Folio 18: De Bacquoy to [Williamson]. Indication that Louis XIV hopes to mediate between England...
description: Folio 18: De Bacquoy to [Williamson]. Indication that Louis XIV hopes to mediate between England and the United Provinces; Dutch pleased to learn that Admiral Montague's ship is undermanned and the crew complain they have not been paid and lack victuals; Dutch plan to send spies to learn of British preparations and plans. Sweden and Denmark prepare for possibility of war. Zealand has asked that her garrisons be reinforced and that some musketeers be withdrawn from the frontier and redeployed on her warships. Gogh leaves for England with instructions to gather intelligence. Dutch receive a report that English naval preparations seem to have halted, and various ministers, like Downing, would prefer an accommodation to a war; however English subjects abroad have been ordered to return home and travelling abroad has been forbidden. Dutch arrange to meet and escort home their East Indies fleet. Other naval preparations are being made discreetly and Dutch warships are not putting to sea to avoid an accidental starting of the war or provoking an English attack. Dutch wish that England should reveal herself to France and other countries as the aggressor if war should break out. Dutch negotiation with Portugal over Cochin and Cananor and with Denmark over disputes in West Africa. Provinces asked to pay a special contribution for additional warships and crews. Brandenburg demands that Dutch settle the Hoef-ÿsser debt. French troops sent to [assist the Emperor] are to be taught German, dictionaries are to be distributed amongst the officers in the hope that by overcoming language barriers the French and German troops can be brought to an harmonie compatible. Turks vanquish imperial army at Canissa. States General are very angry to hear that the English have seized Cape Verde and three Dutch West Indies vessels, directly contrary to Charles II's promises. Date and place: 1660 June 14 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].
context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).

title: Government Code and Cypher School: Diplomatic Section and predecessors: Decrypts of Intercepted Diplomatic Communications (BJ Series)
description: This series contains decrypted foreign diplomatic telegrams and reports by the Government Code and Cypher School. The origin of the series name 'BJ Reports' is that the reports were circulated by the Foreign Office (the main recipient) in blue file jackets. The records referred to as JUMBO reports are based on overseas interception (and often decryption), which could be received by telegraph or by courier from other authorities such as British forces in the Middle East, India and Hong Kong, which practised signals intelligence for their own purposes. They forwarded material of high interest to London. The material up to the end of 1925 covers such subjects as the Russian Civil War and subsequent Soviet negotiations for recognition; post-war settlements in Central and Eastern Europe; the occupation of Turkey and the Graeco-Turkish war; Great Power ambitions in the Middle East; Japanese ambitions in China and the Russian Far East; French intransigence on the questions of German reparations and European security; the rise to power of Mussolini and his increasingly aggressive political tactics to establish Italy as a Great Power. 1926 to 1929 covers Mussolini's growth in power and influence in the Balkans and Eastern Mediterranean and Italian aspirations in North and East Africa and Arabia; civil war in China and her attempts to throw off the control of foreign powers; civil war in Afghanistan and Russian penetration; the Kellogg Non-Aggression Pact and British, American and Japanese diplomatic consultations in preparation for the International Conference on Reduction of Naval Forces and related decrypts issued during the period of the conference from January to April 1930. The years 1939-1945 are concerned almost exclusively with the conduct of the war.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Diplomatic Section and predecessors: Decrypts of Intercepted Diplomatic Communications (BJ Series).

liaison with Russia, Col Crankshaw arrives back in Moscow from UK via ME Aug 24, to fly to Murmansk Sept 1 to liaise with Naval Sigint; liaison with AM, WO, C-in-C West Africa and South Africa; correspondence with CBME, charter for Director CBME Aug 26, cryptic letters from Director CBME to HAS, cover situation in Med area on German, Italian, French and Spanish air tasks; UK guide on identification of German traffic sent to US Army Sigint in UK; report by F/O RE Gunn of RAF Cheadle who led Sigint team on HMS Nelson en route from UK to Med and return July 31-Aug 25 with Malta relief convoy, special Sigint operation at Gibraltar to support team on HMS Nelson Aug 6-20; capture of German Sigint unit west of El Alamein July 10, interrogation of German Sigint officer; BP to GOC-in-C West Africa Accra giving instructions for handling all Sigint reports previously annotated Special in future to be given prefix Ultra; AS letters to AM on RAF manning and promotions; serious staffing problems in Hut 3, Wing Cdr Jones to EWT; Major HB Sayer to be promoted to Lt Col and take new W/T coordination post at BP Aug 4; minutes of AGD's Heads of Sections' meeting of Aug 1; Col Tiltman's Sigint course at Bedford, BP lectures for Sigint course at Newbold Revel Rugby, selection of RAF candidates for training at Rugby; table illustrating various German codes broken by AS and Major Pritchard during June; BP EP customer distribution lists A, B and C; list of French military cyphers being read as at Aug; Italian military cover problems; Capt H Sandwith of Sigs Department Admiralty to visit BP late Aug before Sigint liaison/inspection visit to Gibraltar, Freetown, Kilindini, South Africa, Melbourne and Washington; letter from DMI, Major Gen FHN Davidson, to C explaining apparent compromise of work of BP in WO recruiting of Sigint recruits following complaint from BP, BP dissatisfied with DMI explanation; Paprika code deception plans Aug 5; allocation of receivers for various E tasks at GPO Station Whitchurch, Mar-Aug 1942; exchanges with Major G Stevens, BP's Sigint representative in Washington, status of US attack on various countries' cyphers, US Ambassador London sending Finnish broadcasts intercepted by BBC to Washington - BP to investigate, Head of Met Party in AS, Dr Mc'Vittie, invited to Washington to advise US Aug 3, liaison with US War and Navy Departments, letters from Capt E Hastings RN in Washington to AGD Aug 6 on UK Sigint liaison matters with US and Canada; minutes of Combined Comms Board Telecommunications Committee Sub-committee on Codes and Cyphers held in Washington Aug 6, liaison with Ottawa, details of Canadian intercept sent to BP; liaison with Russia, UK Sigint representative in Moscow, Col Crankshaw, to return to Moscow from UK via ME; correspondence with CBME and other Sigint authorities in ME, tactical use of Sigint in ME, captured Axis documents sent to BP Aug 4, Sigint comms routes to ME, ME concern over E compromise during Sigint training at Cheadle, Director CBME to be transfered to MI-6 to ease problems with Army command chain, Sigint support to C-in-C Med after move to Alexandria Aug 7, supply of Sigint on Axis agents to ME; liaison with UK Sigint in West Africa, with Shaw at Kilindini and with Australia; liaison with WO and AM; liaison with Cheadle and Dunstable on German met problems; BP liaison with Mansfield College Oxford on provision of Type X cypher keys; Z/MSS 7, BP study of GAF intentions against Allied convoys en route from UK to Gibraltar Aug 5; summary of intelligence reports on Allied activities sent from Chile to Berlin during 1942; BP Summary No 8 of enemy intelligence reports July/Aug; AS report to AM on GAF GCI control in Friesian Islands; CX/MSS S13-18 BP reports on German code-names; CX/MSS/1266/TG of Aug 6 BP report on German plans to counter expected major Allied re-supply of Malta; report TR/445 from AM Great Baddow Research Station on enemy PWF signals as jammers.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

description: Hut 6 tasks and staff, headed by WG Welchman; policy paper on interception of E; warning to staff by AGD on dangers of careless talk; liaison with Finns, Lt Col JH Tiltman's report of his visit to Finland Mar 1-11 and his agreement to provide them with Sigint equipment; Y Committee (YC) minutes, Tiltman to be recruiting officer in chief for Services' Sigint recruits; traffic blanketing requirements of Diplomatic and Commercial Sections as submitted to cable censors; support from British Tabulating Machine Company (BTM) for GCCS; Professor TSR Boase to leave BP on Mar 27 for temporary detachment to Cairo on RAF Sigint duties; details of Canadian, South African and French Sigint organisations; French to establish permanent Naval Sigint Mission at BP; Naval Intelligence Department (NID) 9 paper on German illicit spy network, with comments by HC Kenworthy; Y Subcommittee minutes, cover of German illicit morse stations overseas; German illicit activity in South Africa and Portuguese East Africa; MI-8 paper on potential leakage to Germany of British radio communications; War Office (WO) visits to BP and access to Sigint reports, listing of cleared officers; congratulatory message to BP from Director of Naval Intelligence (DNI); minutes of India/ME Intelligence Conference held in Cairo, Apr 3-8, cover of Russian communications; GCCS disagreements with MI-8 and DNI; build up of Services' Sigint Centre in Cairo; details of Italian cypher systems.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

title: Minutes of meeting held at BP on Mar 23 and attended by key BP personnel...
description: Minutes of meeting held at BP on Mar 23 and attended by key BP personnel and representatives from WO, AM and Admiralty, detailed report on visit by DMI, Major General FHN Davidson, to BP on Mar 27; request from AD (S) to Section Heads asking for staff togo to a 2-watch system, enabling all sections to be manned 0900 - midnight; BP communications; Bombe processing hours for period Mar 1-25 by E key family, list of all E keys by area illustrating respective values to Allied intelligence; list of German Army and AF codes showing extent of exploitation and types of intelligence gained, WO E priorities; cypher research problems, ISOS and ISK cypher problems; staff for GCCS and Hut 3, reorganisation of work in Hut 3 with request for increased RAF establishment, recruitment of service personnel for Hut 3; AM reprimands HAS for his views on increasing RAF complement in AS for tasks which AM considered could be done by civilians; terms of reference of the Phoenix Section; immediate Sigint reporting to be done by SALU Section, SALU reporting changes; proposed new form of daily activity report for semi-processed material; GCCS visit to PO station at Whitchurch, found to be indescribably filthy; PO technicians to be transferred to BP; detachment of BP officers to GHQ for Sigint exercise; HAS's course assessment for No 3 Special Intelligence Course held for first time at No 50 Signals Depot, Newbold Revel, Mar 16-28; further requisitioning of accommodation for BP Wrens at Wavendon House, Wavendon; report on captured intercept documents of German Sigint Service with comments by AW Bonsall and PG Lucas of BP; liaison with South Africa and with Australian Sigint organisation at Melbourne, Sigint liaison with Colombo, correspondence with censor in Mauritius; BP correspondence with West Africa Command, correspondence with CBME, Type X Sigint channels to Alexandria and West Africa, liaison with Gibraltar, 7-page report from Director CBME on developments and problems in Bureau, sent with Captain Dryden on liaison visit to BP, comments by AGD on Lt Col Jacob's report, tip-off service from Cheadle to ME, HAS's comments on officer selection for ME Sigint units; correspondence for SIS and SOE; RAF Sigint personnel overseas requirements for 1942, proposed establishment for new Sigint Wing in ME and personnel listings for Sigint units in course of formation, Cheadle comments on personnel listings for these units; proposal to commission in RAF all T/Junior Assistants at Cheadle; deployment of Army operators in UK, additional sets at Harpendon; GCCS criticism of lax RT security by RAF aircraft en route to or operating from Malta, suggestions for improvement.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

title: Minutes of Meeting Number 116 of 1950. 1) Strength of the Garrison in Tripolitania. 2)...
description: Minutes of Meeting Number 116 of 1950. 1) Strength of the Garrison in Tripolitania. 2) Weapon Sites and Installations (Heavy Crossbow) in Northern France. 3) Arms for Yugoslavia. 4) Exercise "Triade". 5) Security Checks within the Metric System. 6) Future of Joint Services Staff College. 7) Defence Talks with the South African Government. 8) Staff Talks with the French in West Africa. 9) Disclosure of Information to the Italians about Co-ordinated Emergency War Plans for the Allied Occupation Forces in Austria and Trieste. 10) Draft Directive to Chiefs of Staff Representative with General Macarthur. 11) Planning of Balanced Forces in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation. 12) Air Reconnaissance: Middle East. 13) Probable Form and Scale of Attack Against ANZAM area - Report by the Joint Intelligence Committee Melbourne. 14) Planning - Defence of Sea Communications in the Australian Home Waters. 15) Meeting of Standing Group. 16) Visit of CIGS to New Zealand. 17) Operation Research Group - Malaya. 18) Discussions with US authorities on Cypher Policy. 19) Naval Command in Western Europe in War. 20) Implications of an Advance of the Possible Date of Outbreak of War.
context: Ministry of Defence: Chiefs of Staff Committee: Minutes. Chiefs of Staff Committee: Minutes of Meetings Nos 116 - 130. (Described at item level)....

title: Paper from WG Welchman to Lt Col Sayer recommending transfer of Capt Lewis's TA party...
description: Paper from WG Welchman to Lt Col Sayer recommending transfer of Capt Lewis's TA party to Hut 6; WG Welchman's summary of his training syllabus for new girls to be employed in the three main areas of Hut 6; EWT writes to MI-8 complaining about treatment of Y Service in WO, too much basic general signals mentality and not enough specialist Y, minute from EWT to C on insecurity of French cyphers still being used in North Africa after armistice with Allies, EWT reprimands Cdr Saunders for sending letter criticising state of Sigint channels direct to Chairman of Y Committee by-passing EWT, confidential report on Cdr Saunders by EWT, sent to Cdr Loehnis at Admiralty; letters from Professor ER Vincent to AD (S) at BP and P Loxley of FO on his possible move to PWE, Sir Alexander Cadogan at FO writes to EWT on impending transfer of Vincent at BP to Italian Section at MWE Woburn, reply from EWT Nov 19 stating Vincent had changed mind and wished to remain at BP; AGD's summary of diplomatic tasks being intercepted and processed by Washington, New Delhi and Melbourne; staff recruitment and retention, correspondence with Oxford University; careless talk security investigations, security vetting procedures; meetings on outgoing comms from BP ordered by C, Cdr Saunders to represent EWT, C subsequently considers standing committee unnecessary but Chairman Y Committee still responsible and Chairman will consult with appropriate officers as required, paper on distribution of Sigint, recommending expansion of SCU system; UK Sigint expansion; minute from Col Tiltman to EWT criticising US cypher procedures; Lt Col Sayer to MI-8 on low priority given to date on works' contracts at WOYG, reply from Sigs 4 via MI-8 Dec 18; pay of AS personnel, tasks for named staff and staffing requirements for parts of AS, AS report of Research and Exploitation Nov 1-15, typing arrangements for BMP report from AS, weekly RAF cover returns for BP; RAF jamming of GAF night fighter comms; NS Memorandum No 94, Report on RFP Identities; complement of Wrens for Stanmore, WRNS postings, Old Rectory North Crawley Bucks requisitioned as accommodation for Wrens Dec 16; new hostel for BP female civilians, located just outside main gate, to open Nov 23; letter from HC Kenworthy at Knockholt to Lt Col Sayer at BP giving operating characteristics of German non-morse equipment, Tunny cover at St Albans; DOE between RSS and BP, liaison visit to RSS Hanslope planned for Nov 24, to RSS Barnet Nov 27; French Resistance decodes send by AD (S) to MI-6; requirement for telephone link between BP and Wick; details of certain PO Sigint operators employed at Brora and Sandridge, report on PO technicians working for BP; selection of candidates from Eire for ISSIS Course; DF Coordination Meeting Dec 20, Dr Barfield appointed as consultant to DF Coordination Section Dec 17, figures of merit for DF stations at Chacewater and Helston, new operators for DF Exchange to visit RSS Barnet and BP, maintenance of HF Adcock DF stations; copy of captured German Army frequency chart; list of Sigint world-wide addresses and signal prefixes; submarine cable arrangements to serve Allied bases in NW Africa; UK Sigint assets in ME and PAIFORCE; Sigint associated with Allied landings of Nov 8 in Morocco and Algeria, Vichy instructing French forces to fight to the last; liaison with US War and Naval Departments, Admiralty signal to Navy Department on German instruction to U-boats not to attack in given zone, probably that taken by outward bound blockade runners, EWT's correspondence with Maidment and Bayly of BSC NY and with Major Stevens in Washington, Stevens signals EWT Nov 20 on future meeting of Combined Intelligence Sub-Committee in Washington on Dec 1 to discuss proposal of British Joint Chiefs for mutual vetting of Allied cypher systems, correspondence between Stevens and Col Tiltman and AGD at BP, letters between Kendrick in Ottawa and AGD, correspondence with CBME, AS gives RAF Sigint effort in Med area to Director CBME Nov 15, BP support to 351 WU Gibraltar, some personnel to move from Gibraltar to Algiers, 380 WU to open up in Algiers; liaison with Col Crankshaw in Moscow, no Sigint cooperation by Soviets since Oct 2, Crankshaw wishes to threaten withdrawal of UK Sigint representative from Moscow, meeting at Polyarnoe between RN, RAF and Soviet Naval Sigint representatives Nov 15; liaison with South Africa, Capt Sandwith RN visits South African DDMI in Pretoria Nov 20; liaison with Shaw in Kilindini, Merry in Melbourne, GOC West Africa, AF HQ West Africa Freetown, 371 WU Freetown, AM and WO; BP EP, CX/MSS/S 32 Reported Locations of German RDF Apparatus in North Africa, EX/SALU 12 GAF Operations in Areas of Air Fleets 3 and 5, SDE/TS6 German Experimental Activity Oct 1942, CX/MSS/ZTPG/87615 (1699/2) Italian Admiral to Command Axis Liaison with French Navy at Toulon, summary of SALU 3G output and terms of reference May-Nov 1942.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

EWTnotes for BP security officers; security and reliability of Hollerith encyphering machine, modification of Type X equipment, Type X equipment for BP; letter from Gordon Welchman, Head of Hut 6, to Nigel de Grey, (AD (S) apologising for his outburst earlier that day, summarises Hut 6 problems which mainly revolved around the morale of his female staff; BP reports on German Sigint Organisation, 6 IS report on German Sigint DF organisation; 3 ATS decoders for Hut 6 to be detached to GHQ Home Forces in event of invasion; MEW letter to AGD asking for more Sigint from Canada on Far East; Director WRNS and WRNS Superintendent The Nore to visit BP on June 8, case for commissioning some BP Wrens, new officer posts required for supervision; access of RSS officer Capt Trevor-Roper to BP, EWT to C agreeing to ban him, support from SIS, RSS Group 8 Italian net subject for disagreement between Trevor Roper and GCCS, RSS intercepts Soviet diplomatic traffic; French Resistance traffic sent to SIS from GCCS; handling of ISOS material both at BP and in ME; new aerial to improve reception at PO station at Brora; liaison with Colombo, India and Canada, 21-page report on Canadian Sigint organisation by Capt HR Sandwith of British Admiralty, compiled at Ottawa during his visit to North America for the CANUKUS Sigint Conference in Washington; correspondence with CBME, case for continuing Sigint in Malta, Air Marshal Tedder's assessment of German ME plans - to capture Malta, congratulatory signal to BP from Air Marshal Tedder, AOC-in-C ME, German intentions in ME - a Sigint appreciation, JIC (MEF) assessment of German intentions in Libya based on BP Sigint reports, results of monitoring exercise on British military comms in ME and W Africa with recommendations for improvements, German Sigint reports on RAF delivery flights to Gibraltar - evaluation by AM AI 4B, RSS and GCCS cover in ME, results of monitoring exercise on British military comms in ME and W Africa with recommendations for improvements; YC note on German development of non-morse comms; agenda for Inter-Services Cypher Security Committee meeting, security of UK cypher systems; support for Bomber Command from RAF Kingsdown; monitoring of Coastal Command air/ground comms by RAF Cheadle; context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

title: EWT orders details of new GCCS reorganisation to be sent to Director CBME Lt Col...
description: EWT orders details of new GCCS reorganisation to be sent to Director CBME Lt Col Jacob in Cairo, to Shaw in Colombo, to Strachey in Ottawa and Hastings in Washington; EWT asks FO if new AD (A) Cdr Bradshaw can become an FO official; AGD asks C whether PMand FO would wish him to pass back decrypted diplomatic traffic to US as US censors were passing all neutral diplomatic raw traffic to us for processing; EWT paper on reorganisation of Military and Air Force work at BP; re-allocation of rooms at BP, Diplomatic Section to move from Elmers School to Wavendon and ISOS/ISK and Italian Military Section to replace it at Elmers; new Mess Committee meets on Feb 28 chaired by AD (A); minutes of Hut 3 Committee meeting chaired by AD (S) confirming implentation of new orders, suggestions for improving record keeping and TA in Hut 3, GSO 2 to be appointed as military representative in Hut 3, new orders for Hut 3 RAF personnel by Wing Cdr RH Humphreys with covering note to EWT; sorting of raw material at BP wef Mar 1, order on subject from EWT; letter to FO requesting Treasury funds for Kenworthy's research work into German teleprinters; traffic flow statistics for BP Cypher Office; telephone and teleprinter lines into BP, BP telephone security; cyphers for UK Sigint channels; contingency plan for taking over PO diplomatic cover positions for military tasks in event of invasion of UK; proposed totals of Sigint positions by target country by end of 1942; C requests limited distribution for ISOS/ISK messages referring to Allied agents, BP standing orders for handling of ISOS/ISK material tip-off service in advance of reporting, (SO Nos 1-5); RAF Air Cdr to visit BP and inspect new WAAF hostel at Shenley Park; course reports for No 2 Sigint Course at Buckingham Feb 3-13, RAF Sigint courses, previously held at Buckingham to be held at 50 Signals Depot RAF Newbold Revel; WRNS postings; new UK representative to Moscow for Sigint liaison with Russians, liaison with South Africa, liaison with Free French Sigint; correspondence with CBME, mainly between HAS and Director CBME, ME Censorship Service providing diplomatic traffic for GCCS, GCCS correspondence with 51 WIU Gibraltar, AM representatives from DDI 4 to visit 51 WIU, Comsec violations by Free French in ME; use of Sigint by MI-8; DMI asks EWT for more Sigint on Axis plans for Russia and ME; Naval Y Service expansion progress report for Jan/Feb 1942; DDI 4 orders visit to Dunstable Met Sigint Unit to look for ways of improving analysis liaison with BP; expansion of RAF Sigint in Levant and Iraq; feed back to operators at RAF Y stations, Sigint security lecture; signals plan for GAF units in Norway; German Abwehr links to German legations and consulates.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

description: DMI and CIGS to visit BP on Apr 16, programme for visit; letter from EWT to C on opportunities lost because GCCS not tipped off in advance about Allied war plans; paper by Lt Cdr AG Saunders, previously Head of Hut 3, on his proposals for re-organisationof GCCS, case for 5 Controllers or Divisional Heads respectively in charge of intercept, cryptography, intelligence, communications and security, and UK Comsec, supporting chart illustrated GCCS Sigint sources and processing chains; detailed summary by AD (S) on staff shortages in various areas of BP, staff shortages as at Feb 2 in PS Milner-Barry's section, WG Welchman's minute to EWT on staff shortages in Hut 6; organisation within Hut 6, outlook for Hut 6 processing, 1942-1943; statistics for work processing in Huts 3 and 6 as at Apr 13, measures to reduce backlog in Hut 3; liaison between SALU and Day Fighter Sections; handling of Abwehr Orange key material after leaving Hut 6; fortnightly section reports, NS too busy to participate; support from BTM, special tabulating machines at BP in future to be known as Cantabs, details of future supply and working of Cantabs; requisitioning of Court Haw House for GCCS, probably in association with Metropolitan Police intercept site at Denmark Hill, case for Sigint research by police; case for more Sigint men and equipment to intercept German teleprinter, a developing problem for BP; results of 4th Special Sigint Course at 50 Signals Depot, Mar 30-Apr 10; AS report on GAF reaction to RAF attack on Hazebrouck, Apr 12; report on GAF developments from Wing Cdr Humphries at BP to Gp Capt Winterbotham at AM; liaison with South Africa, Canada, Russia, and COIS Colombo; correspondence with CBME, personnel for 54 WU in ME; Sigint report on GAF Little Screw beacon position indicator system; build up of GAF transport aircraft in Eastern Prussia, GAF crack Air Corps withdrawn from Russian Front, Central Sector; letter from US General to AM putting case for common US/UK communications and cypher systems; copy of Act 814 of ACI of Apr 18, all Army cypher personnel to transfer to Royal Signals; letter from R Baudouin, working for GCCS, to Col Friedman of US Army Sigint, on Friedman's request on behalf of the War Department for 1000 copies of Baudouin's book Elements de Cryptographie.
context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.

context: Government Code and Cypher School: Directorate: Second World War Policy Papers.
